    Verify L'Hôpital's hypotheses: as x→∞x \to \inftyx→∞, ln⁡x→∞\ln x \to \inftylnx→∞ and x1/2→∞x^{1/2} \to \inftyx1/2→∞, so this is an ∞∞\frac{\infty}{\infty}∞∞​ form.

  3. By the limit-000 case of the limit comparison test: if anbn→0\frac{a_n}{b_n} \to 0bn​an​​→0 and ∑bn\sum b_n∑bn​ converges, then ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ converges. Hence ∑n=2∞ln⁡nn2\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{\ln n}{n^2}∑n=2∞​n2lnn​ converges.

2Easy

For N≥2N \ge 2N≥2, evaluate the partial product PN=∏n=2N(1−1n2)P_N = \prod_{n=2}^{N}\left(1-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)PN​=∏n=2N​(1−n21​) and prove lim⁡N→∞PN=12\lim_{N\to\infty} P_N = \frac{1}{2}limN→∞​PN​=21​.

PN=N+12N→12P_N = \frac{N+1}{2N} \to \frac{1}{2}PN​=2NN+1​→21​
  • Telescoping Series
  • Wallis Product
Show solution

  1. Since 1−1n2=n2−1n2=(n−1)(n+1)n21-\frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{n^2-1}{n^2} = \frac{(n-1)(n+1)}{n^2}1−n21​=n2n2−1​=n2(n−1)(n+1)​, split the product in two: PN=∏n=2Nn−1n⋅∏n=2Nn+1nP_N = \prod_{n=2}^{N}\frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\prod_{n=2}^{N}\frac{n+1}{n}PN​=∏n=2N​nn−1​⋅∏n=2N​nn+1​.

  2. The first product telescopes: 12⋅23⋯N−1N=1N\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdots\frac{N-1}{N} = \frac{1}{N}21​⋅32​⋯NN−1​=N1​. So does the second: 32⋅43⋯N+1N=N+12\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\cdots\frac{N+1}{N} = \frac{N+1}{2}23​⋅34​⋯NN+1​=2N+1​.

  3. Hence PN=1N⋅N+12=N+12N=12+12N→12P_N = \frac{1}{N}\cdot\frac{N+1}{2} = \frac{N+1}{2N} = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2N} \to \frac{1}{2}PN​=N1​⋅2N+1​=2NN+1​=21​+2N1​→21​. So the infinite product ∏n=2∞(1−1n2)\prod_{n=2}^{\infty}\left(1-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)∏n=2∞​(1−n21​) converges to 12\frac{1}{2}21​.

Show that ∑n=1∞(−1)n+1n(n+1)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n(n+1)}∑n=1∞​n(n+1)(−1)n+1​ converges, compute the third partial sum S3S_3S3​, and bound the remainder ∣S−S3∣|S - S_3|∣S−S3​∣.

S3=12−16+112=512,∣S−S3∣≤120S_3 = \frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{12} = \frac{5}{12}, \qquad |S-S_3| \le \frac{1}{20}S3​=21​−61​+121​=125​,∣S−S3​∣≤201​

Show solution

  3. The alternating-series error bound gives ∣S−S3∣≤b4=14⋅5=120=0.05|S - S_3| \le b_4 = \frac{1}{4\cdot 5} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.05∣S−S3​∣≤b4​=4⋅51​=201​=0.05. So SSS lies within 0.050.050.05 of 512\frac{5}{12}125​.

4Medium

Explain why the ratio test is inconclusive for ∑n=1∞(2n)!4n(n!)2⋅1n\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(2n)!}{4^n (n!)^2}\cdot\frac{1}{n}∑n=1∞​4n(n!)2(2n)!​⋅n1​, then prove convergence with Raabe's test.

n(1−an+1an)=n(3n+2)2(n+1)2→32>1n\left(1-\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right) = \frac{n(3n+2)}{2(n+1)^2} \to \frac{3}{2} > 1n(1−an​an+1​​)=2(n+1)2n(3n+2)​→23​>1
  • Raabe's Test
  • Convergence Tests Toolbox
Show solution

  1. Put an=(2n)!4n(n!)2⋅1n>0a_n = \frac{(2n)!}{4^n (n!)^2}\cdot\frac{1}{n} > 0an​=4n(n!)2(2n)!​⋅n1​>0. Then an+1an=(2n+2)(2n+1)4⋅1(n+1)2⋅nn+1=n(2n+1)2(n+1)2→1\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}\cdot\frac{n}{n+1} = \frac{n(2n+1)}{2(n+1)^2} \to 1an​an+1​​=4(2n+2)(2n+1)​⋅(n+1)21​⋅n+1n​=2(n+1)2n(2n+1)​→1, so the ratio test is inconclusive.

  2. Compute the Raabe quantity: 1−an+1an=2(n+1)2−n(2n+1)2(n+1)2=3n+22(n+1)21-\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{2(n+1)^2-n(2n+1)}{2(n+1)^2} = \frac{3n+2}{2(n+1)^2}1−an​an+1​​=2(n+1)22(n+1)2−n(2n+1)​=2(n+1)23n+2​, hence n(1−an+1an)=n(3n+2)2(n+1)2→32n\left(1-\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right) = \frac{n(3n+2)}{2(n+1)^2} \to \frac{3}{2}n(1−an​an+1​​)=2(n+1)2n(3n+2)​→23​.

  3. The chapter's Raabe form is n(anan+1−1)n\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - 1\right)n(an+1​an​​−1); the two limits agree: since an+1an→1\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \to 1an​an+1​​→1, n(anan+1−1)=n(1−an+1an)⋅anan+1n\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - 1\right) = n\left(1 - \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right)\cdot\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}n(an+1​an​​−1)=n(1−an​an+1​​)⋅an+1​an​​ and the extra factor anan+1→1\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} \to 1an+1​an​​→1, so both limits are the same.

    Since the limit 32>1\frac{3}{2} > 123​>1, Raabe's test gives convergence of ∑an\sum a_n∑an​.

    (Indeed (2nn)∼4nπn\binom{2n}{n} \sim \frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi n}}(n2n​)∼πn​4n​, so an∼1π n3/2a_n \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}\,n^{3/2}}an​∼π​n3/21​.)

5Medium

Prove that ∑n=2∞(−1)n n+(−1)nn \sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{\,n+(-1)^n\sqrt{n}\,}∑n=2∞​n+(−1)nn​(−1)n​ converges conditionally.

(Hint: use 11+u=1−u+u21+u\frac{1}{1+u} = 1-u+\frac{u^2}{1+u}1+u1​=1−u+1+uu2​.)

(−1)nn+(−1)nn=(−1)nn−1n3/2+σn,∣σn∣≤Cn2\frac{(-1)^n}{n+(-1)^n\sqrt{n}} = \frac{(-1)^n}{n}-\frac{1}{n^{3/2}}+\sigma_n, \quad |\sigma_n| \le \frac{C}{n^2}n+(−1)nn​(−1)n​=n(−1)n​−n3/21​+σn​,∣σn​∣≤n2C​
  • Leibniz Series
  • Convergence Tests Toolbox
Show solution

  1. Put bn=1n+(−1)nn>0b_n = \frac{1}{n+(-1)^n\sqrt{n}} > 0bn​=n+(−1)nn​1​>0 (n≥2n \ge 2n≥2).

    Factoring nnn from the denominator, bn=1n⋅11+unb_n = \frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{1+u_n}bn​=n1​⋅1+un​1​ with un=(−1)nnu_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}un​=n​(−1)n​, ∣un∣≤12|u_n| \le \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}∣un​∣≤2​1​.

    The bound gives un≥−12>−1u_n \ge -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} > -1un​≥−2​1​>−1, so 1+un≥1−12>01 + u_n \ge 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} > 01+un​≥1−2​1​>0; hence un≠−1u_n \ne -1un​=−1 and the hint's identity 11+un=1−un+un21+un\frac{1}{1+u_n} = 1-u_n+\frac{u_n^2}{1+u_n}1+un​1​=1−un​+1+un​un2​​ is valid.

    The identity therefore gives 11+un=1−un+ρn\frac{1}{1+u_n} = 1-u_n+\rho_n1+un​1​=1−un​+ρn​ where ∣ρn∣=un2∣1+un∣≤Cn|\rho_n| = \frac{u_n^2}{|1+u_n|} \le \frac{C}{n}∣ρn​∣=∣1+un​∣un2​​≤nC​ with C=11−1/2C = \frac{1}{1-1/\sqrt{2}}C=1−1/2​1​.

  2. Hence (−1)nbn=(−1)nn−(−1)nunn+(−1)nρnn(-1)^n b_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{n}-\frac{(-1)^n u_n}{n}+\frac{(-1)^n\rho_n}{n}(−1)nbn​=n(−1)n​−n(−1)nun​​+n(−1)nρn​​, and since (−1)nun=1n(-1)^n u_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(−1)nun​=n​1​, we get (−1)nbn=(−1)nn−1n3/2+σn(-1)^n b_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{n}-\frac{1}{n^{3/2}}+\sigma_n(−1)nbn​=n(−1)n​−n3/21​+σn​ with ∣σn∣≤Cn2|\sigma_n| \le \frac{C}{n^2}∣σn​∣≤n2C​. The three series ∑(−1)nn\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n}∑n(−1)n​ (alternating series test), ∑1n3/2\sum\frac{1}{n^{3/2}}∑n3/21​ (ppp-series), and ∑σn\sum\sigma_n∑σn​ (absolutely convergent) all converge, so ∑(−1)nbn\sum (-1)^n b_n∑(−1)nbn​ converges.

  3. It does not converge absolutely: n+(−1)nn≤n+n≤2nn+(-1)^n\sqrt{n} \le n+\sqrt{n} \le 2nn+(−1)nn​≤n+n​≤2n (n≥1n \ge 1n≥1), so bn≥12nb_n \ge \frac{1}{2n}bn​≥2n1​, and ∑12n\sum\frac{1}{2n}∑2n1​ diverges; by comparison ∑bn\sum b_n∑bn​ diverges too. Hence the convergence is conditional.

Hard

6Hard

For real ppp, prove by applying the condensation test twice that the Bertrand series ∑n=3∞1n ln⁡n (ln⁡ln⁡n)p\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n\,\ln n\,(\ln\ln n)^p}∑n=3∞​nlnn(lnlnn)p1​ converges if and only if p>1p > 1p>1.

∑2na2n=∑n≥31ln⁡2⋅n (ln⁡(nln⁡2))p≍∑n≥31n(ln⁡n)p\sum 2^n a_{2^n} = \sum_{n\ge 3}\frac{1}{\ln 2\cdot n\,(\ln(n\ln 2))^p} \asymp \sum_{n\ge 3}\frac{1}{n(\ln n)^p}∑2na2n​=n≥3∑​ln2⋅n(ln(nln2))p1​≍n≥3∑​n(lnn)p1​
  • Cauchy Condensation Test
  • Convergence Tests Toolbox
Show solution

  1. Put an=1n ln⁡n (ln⁡ln⁡n)pa_n = \frac{1}{n\,\ln n\,(\ln\ln n)^p}an​=nlnn(lnlnn)p1​ (n≥3n \ge 3n≥3).

    Treat only p≥0p \ge 0p≥0 by condensation first: for n≥3n \ge 3n≥3, ln⁡ln⁡n>0\ln\ln n > 0lnlnn>0, nnn and ln⁡n\ln nlnn are positive and increasing, and for p≥0p \ge 0p≥0 so is (ln⁡ln⁡n)p(\ln\ln n)^p(lnlnn)p; hence ana_nan​ decreases monotonically to 000.

    The condensation test applies.

    (For p<0p < 0p<0, (ln⁡ln⁡n)p(\ln\ln n)^p(lnlnn)p is decreasing and the monotonicity claim is false — e.g. for p=−1p = -1p=−1, a3≈0.0285<a4≈0.0589a_3 \approx 0.0285 < a_4 \approx 0.0589a3​≈0.0285<a4​≈0.0589. The case p<0p < 0p<0 is handled in the last step by comparison alone, with no condensation.)

  2. First condensation: 2na2n=1ln⁡2⋅n (ln⁡(nln⁡2))p2^n a_{2^n} = \frac{1}{\ln 2\cdot n\,(\ln(n\ln 2))^p}2na2n​=ln2⋅n(ln(nln2))p1​. Since ln⁡(nln⁡2)=ln⁡n+ln⁡ln⁡2\ln(n\ln 2) = \ln n+\ln\ln 2ln(nln2)=lnn+lnln2 with ln⁡ln⁡2≈−0.3665\ln\ln 2 \approx -0.3665lnln2≈−0.3665, we have 12ln⁡n≤ln⁡(nln⁡2)≤ln⁡n\frac{1}{2}\ln n \le \ln(n\ln 2) \le \ln n21​lnn≤ln(nln2)≤lnn for n≥3n \ge 3n≥3 (the upper bound from ln⁡2<1\ln 2 < 1ln2<1; the lower from 12ln⁡n≥−ln⁡ln⁡2\frac{1}{2}\ln n \ge -\ln\ln 221​lnn≥−lnln2, true for n≥3n \ge 3n≥3).

  3. For p>0p > 0p>0 these two-sided bounds make the condensed series comparable, up to constants, to ∑n≥31n(ln⁡n)p\sum_{n\ge 3}\frac{1}{n(\ln n)^p}∑n≥3​n(lnn)p1​ (comparison test).

    Re-verify the condensation hypotheses for the second application: for p>0p > 0p>0, bn=1n(ln⁡n)pb_n = \frac{1}{n(\ln n)^p}bn​=n(lnn)p1​ is positive, and since nnn and (ln⁡n)p(\ln n)^p(lnn)p are both positive and increasing, bnb_nbn​ decreases monotonically to 000 — so condensation applies again.

    Condensing again gives ∑2n⋅12n(nln⁡2)p=1(ln⁡2)p∑1np\sum 2^n\cdot\frac{1}{2^n(n\ln 2)^p} = \frac{1}{(\ln 2)^p}\sum\frac{1}{n^p}∑2n⋅2n(nln2)p1​=(ln2)p1​∑np1​, which converges only for p>1p > 1p>1.

    Hence for p>0p > 0p>0 we get convergence when p>1p > 1p>1 and divergence when 0<p≤10 < p \le 10<p≤1.

  4. The case p<0p < 0p<0 (and p=0p = 0p=0) is handled by comparison alone — no monotonicity of the original series is needed: if n≥16n \ge 16n≥16 then ln⁡ln⁡n≥1\ln\ln n \ge 1lnlnn≥1 (since n≥ee≈15.15n \ge e^e \approx 15.15n≥ee≈15.15), so (ln⁡ln⁡n)p≤1(\ln\ln n)^p \le 1(lnlnn)p≤1 and an≥1nln⁡na_n \ge \frac{1}{n\ln n}an​≥nlnn1​.

    Since ∑1nln⁡n\sum\frac{1}{n\ln n}∑nlnn1​ diverges (one condensation turns it into a constant multiple of the harmonic series), comparison gives divergence of the original series too.

    Thus convergence holds if and only if p>1p > 1p>1.

7Hard

Using the Euler product, prove that the infinite product ∏p prime(1+1p2)\prod_{p\ \text{prime}}\left(1+\frac{1}{p^2}\right)∏p prime​(1+p21​) converges and equals 15π2\frac{15}{\pi^2}π215​.

(You may use ζ(2)=π26\zeta(2) = \frac{\pi^2}{6}ζ(2)=6π2​ and ζ(4)=π490\zeta(4) = \frac{\pi^4}{90}ζ(4)=90π4​ as known.)

∏p≤x(1+1p2)=∏p≤x(1−p−2)−1∏p≤x(1−p−4)−1→ζ(2)ζ(4)=15π2\prod_{p\le x}\left(1+\frac{1}{p^2}\right) = \frac{\prod_{p\le x}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}}{\prod_{p\le x}(1-p^{-4})^{-1}} \to \frac{\zeta(2)}{\zeta(4)} = \frac{15}{\pi^2}p≤x∏​(1+p21​)=∏p≤x​(1−p−4)−1∏p≤x​(1−p−2)−1​→ζ(4)ζ(2)​=π215​
  • The Euler Product
  • The Basel Problem
Show solution

  1. For s>1s > 1s>1 the Euler product ζ(s)=∏p(1−p−s)−1\zeta(s) = \prod_{p}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}ζ(s)=∏p​(1−p−s)−1 holds (understood as the limit of finite partial products). The key identity is 1+1p2=1−p−41−p−21+\frac{1}{p^2} = \frac{1-p^{-4}}{1-p^{-2}}1+p21​=1−p−21−p−4​ — division is legitimate since the denominator is nonzero (p≥2p \ge 2p≥2).

  2. Over the finite set of primes {p≤x}\{p \le x\}{p≤x}, ∏p≤x(1+1p2)=∏p≤x(1−p−4)∏p≤x(1−p−2)=∏p≤x(1−p−2)−1∏p≤x(1−p−4)−1\prod_{p\le x}\left(1+\frac{1}{p^2}\right) = \frac{\prod_{p\le x}(1-p^{-4})}{\prod_{p\le x}(1-p^{-2})} = \frac{\prod_{p\le x}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}}{\prod_{p\le x}(1-p^{-4})^{-1}}∏p≤x​(1+p21​)=∏p≤x​(1−p−2)∏p≤x​(1−p−4)​=∏p≤x​(1−p−4)−1∏p≤x​(1−p−2)−1​. Every factor is positive, so no rearrangement issue arises.

  3. As x→∞x \to \inftyx→∞, the numerator tends to ζ(2)=π26\zeta(2) = \frac{\pi^2}{6}ζ(2)=6π2​ and the denominator to ζ(4)=π490\zeta(4) = \frac{\pi^4}{90}ζ(4)=90π4​ (Euler product).

    The denominator's limit ζ(4)≠0\zeta(4) \ne 0ζ(4)=0 — no factor of the convergent Euler product is zero — so the quotient limit law applies.

    Hence the infinite product converges to π2/6π4/90=906π2=15π2\frac{\pi^2/6}{\pi^4/90} = \frac{90}{6\pi^2} = \frac{15}{\pi^2}π4/90π2/6​=6π290​=π215​.
